opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fun comparison because on the surface they look like the same kind of problem — you have some state, you roll it forward, and small differences compound — but I think they're actually quite different in where the hardness lives.

With weather, the chaos is physical. You have a system that's genuinely sensitive to initial conditions in the Lorenz sense, and the problem is that you can never measure the initial state precisely enough. Every sensor has noise, you don't have coverage everywhere, and those tiny errors grow exponentially. So there's a fundamental horizon — people usually say something like two weeks — beyond which no amount of compute really saves you for deterministic point forecasts. What you can do is shift to predicting distributions: ensembles, probabilistic forecasts, climate statistics rather than whether it rains on a specific Tuesday. And that's actually where a lot of the recent ML weather models have been interesting — they're not breaking the chaos limit, they're getting much cheaper and sometimes more accurate within it, and making large ensembles affordable.

Go is different because you have perfect information. There's no measurement noise; the board state is exactly known. The "chaos," if you want to call it that, is combinatorial — one stone placed differently can flip the life-and-death status of a whole group fifty moves later. So the difficulty isn't that you can't know the present; it's that the branching factor makes brute-force rollout intractable. And what AlphaGo and its successors showed is that you can learn a value function that compresses all that future complexity into an intuition about a position. You don't simulate every line; you learn which positions are good, and then search sparingly around that.

So I think the interesting lesson is: in Go, learned intuition plus search lets you sidestep the combinatorial explosion, because the underlying system is deterministic and fully observed. In weather, you can learn better models of the dynamics, but you're still bounded by the information you have about the present. The ceiling is set by observation, not by compute.

And I think that distinction matters a lot when people talk about AI predicting things like markets, or geopolitics, or human behavior. You have to ask: is this hard because the search space is big — in which case learning plus compute might crack it — or is it hard because the system is chaotic and partially observed — in which case the best you'll ever do is a well-calibrated distribution? A lot of hype comes from treating the second kind of problem as if it were the first.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Go’s combinatorial difficulty with weather’s chaos and says learned value functions can assess positions, but it does not state that the winner can be predicted when the exact future board state cannot.

r002.rationale: The response makes no comparison between chaotic systems and hash functions, or between their macroscopic structure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the interesting thing is that chaos isn't really one thing, it's more like a spectrum of how fast your uncertainty grows, and Go and weather sit at pretty different points on it.

With weather, you have this physical system where tiny perturbations in the initial conditions double in magnitude on some fairly short timescale, and the system is also kind of smooth and continuous, so there's no way to exploit structure to get around that. You can keep throwing compute and sensors at it, and you push the horizon out maybe a day per decade, but the fundamental thing is that you're fighting an exponential. The information you'd need to predict two weeks out just isn't in the measurements you can take, and no amount of modeling cleverness conjures it back. So I think of weather as genuinely limited by chaos in the physics sense.

Go feels different to me even though people sometimes describe it with the same language, like "a single stone changes everything." The game is deterministic, the state is fully observable, and the branching factor is huge, but the chaos there isn't about measurement noise, it's about the opponent. If you ask "who wins this game," the uncertainty is almost entirely about what the players are going to do, not about whether you can see the board. And what AlphaGo and later systems showed is that a lot of what looked like irreducible complexity was actually learnable structure. A strong value network can look at a position and say, this is 70-30, and it's pretty well calibrated. That's a kind of prediction that would be impossible in the weather case because there's no equivalent of a value function that compresses the future of the atmosphere.

So the framing I like is: chaos sets a limit on predicting trajectories, but it doesn't necessarily set a limit on predicting outcomes or distributions. In weather we've sort of accepted this and moved to ensemble forecasts, probability of rain rather than "it will rain at 3pm." In Go, the exact sequence of moves is unpredictable but the win probability is very predictable. And I think a lot of the robotics and AI work I care about lives in that gap. You can't predict exactly how a cup is going to slip out of a gripper, but you can predict that this grasp is bad with high confidence, and that's usually enough to act well.

The place where this gets philosophically interesting is when you ask how much of the apparent chaos in a system is really chaos versus just not having the right representation yet. Pre-AlphaGo, if you'd asked a Go pro how predictable a mid-game position is, they'd say it's very hard, lots of variance. It turned out that difficulty was partly a limitation of human pattern recognition. Weather, I'm much more confident is real chaos, because we understand the equations and we can measure the Lyapunov exponents directly. But I try to stay humble about which bucket any given hard problem falls into.

r001.rationale: It says the exact sequence of Go moves is unpredictable while the win probability is very predictable.

r002.rationale: It discusses structure in weather and Go but does not mention hash functions or their intended lack of predictable macroscopic structure.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish predicting the exact trajectory from predicting something useful about the outcome. In weather, tiny differences in the initial conditions can grow until you get very different forecasts. More compute helps, but it doesn’t give you infinitely precise measurements of the initial state. So there’s a limit to how far out you can predict the particular weather, even if you understand the dynamics very well.

Go is a little different because the board is fully observable and the rules are discrete. If you knew both players’ policies and they were deterministic, there wouldn’t be that same uncertainty about the initial conditions. But predicting the actual sequence of moves might still require doing something as computationally expensive as playing the game out.

And you can be good at Go without predicting that sequence. You can look at a position and say, ‘Black has a substantial advantage,’ while having no idea exactly what the board will look like fifty moves later. That’s the distinction I find interesting: a system can be hard to predict in detail while still having enough structure for you to make good decisions.

r001.rationale: It says a player can judge that Black has a substantial advantage without knowing the exact board fifty moves later, conveying outcome-level predictability despite uncertainty about the precise future state.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss hash functions or contrast their intended lack of macroscopic structure with chaotic systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a distinction between predicting the exact trajectory of a system and predicting some property of the outcome. In Go, I might have no idea what sequence of moves two strong players will make, but I can still have a pretty good estimate of who’s going to win. The space of possible games is enormous, but you don’t necessarily have to predict the entire game to evaluate a position.

Weather has a similar distinction. Tiny differences in the initial conditions can eventually lead to very different weather, so there’s a horizon beyond which predicting rain at a particular place and time becomes very difficult. But that doesn’t mean every statistical property becomes unpredictable. You can still say useful things about seasonal patterns or average temperatures.

So when we say chaos limits prediction, the question is: prediction of what, and at what level of detail? A better model can help you approach the limit imposed by uncertainty in your observations. It can’t necessarily eliminate that limit.

r001.rationale: It says the exact sequence of Go moves may be unknown while the likely winner can still be estimated.

r002.rationale: It discusses statistical predictability in weather and Go, but does not mention hash functions or contrast their intended lack of structure with chaotic systems.
